questions.q: What is the problem with identifying stakeholders informally, by who shows up to meetings?
options: It tends to miss people whose objections surface later, after a policy is already written — the most expensive time to find out
It identifies too many stakeholders and wastes time
It only works for very small organizations
It is required by regulation to use a formal method instead
questions.explain: The lesson's core warning: informal identification misses people whose late objections are the costliest to discover.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four directions the lesson says to look when identifying stakeholders?
options: Competitors in the same industry
Data owners and stewards with direct authority
Business units that consume the data
IT, security, legal, and compliance functions
questions.explain: The four directions are owners/stewards, data consumers, IT/legal/compliance, and leadership/external parties — not competitors.

questions.q: On the power/interest grid, how should a stakeholder with high power but low interest be engaged?
options: Keep satisfied — periodic, high-level updates that maintain support without overloading them
Manage closely with daily direct engagement
Ignore them entirely since they have low interest
Put them in charge of writing all policy documents
questions.explain: High power/low interest stakeholders need enough contact to stay supportive, without the heavier engagement reserved for high-interest stakeholders.

options: A documented list naming each stakeholder, what they care about, and how the program's scope affects them
A software tool that automatically governs data
A legal contract stakeholders must sign
The same document as the program charter
questions.explain: The register is the output of the identification step — a documented list, distinct from the charter itself.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say over-engaging a low-power, high-interest stakeholder (like pulling an analyst into every steering committee meeting) is a mistake?
options: Their engagement should match their quadrant — heavy, frequent detail at the right level, not unnecessary high-level meetings that don't fit their actual need
Low-interest stakeholders should never be contacted at all
Only executives are allowed to attend steering committee meetings
Analysts have no role in a governance program
questions.explain: The grid's value comes from matching engagement to the actual quadrant — over- or under-engaging either wastes effort or under-serves a real need.
